Constrained
kon-STRAND
v. (past t. and past part.)
From Latin constringere, to bind together, from con and stringere, to draw tight. Webster 1828: compelled; forced; urged with irresistible power. The root image is a binding that leaves no other course open.

Biblical Definition

Constrained in Scripture describes a pressure that leaves no other course open, and it comes from love as often as from necessity. Two of the loveliest instances are hospitality that would not take no for an answer. The disciples at Emmaus, walking with a stranger who made as though He would go further: But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them (Luke 24:29) — and it was in the breaking of bread that they knew Him. Lydia, newly baptized at Philippi, does the same to Paul’s company: If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there. And she constrained us (Acts 16:15). The word is also used of the Lord’s own hand on His disciples: straightway Jesus constrained his disciples to get into a ship, and to go before him unto the other side (Matthew 14:22) — He sent them deliberately into the storm that followed. And Paul uses it of a legal necessity forced on him by opposition: when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of (Acts 28:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CONSTRAINED as urged with irresistible power or by strong motives; compelled; forced; restrained or confined; also, produced by compulsion and therefore not free or natural.

expand to see more

CONSTRAINED, pp. — Urged with irresistible power or by strong motives; compelled; forced.

Restrained; confined; held back from acting freely.

Produced by compulsion; not voluntary; as, a constrained manner or a constrained assent.

In Scripture, used both of pressing hospitality upon a guest and of a necessity laid on a man by circumstances or by God.

From Latin con and stringo, to draw tight — the root also of strain, restrain, and stringent.

Key Scripture

Luke 24:29 — "But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them."

Acts 16:15 — "And when she was baptized, and her household, she besought us, saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there. And she constrained us."

Matthew 14:22 — "And straightway Jesus constrained his disciples to get into a ship, and to go before him unto the other side, while he sent the multitudes away."

Acts 28:19 — "But when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of."

Modern Corruption

Matthew 14:22 has Christ deliberately putting His disciples into the boat that ran into the storm, which contradicts the widespread assumption that obedience to God’s leading is confirmed by calm conditions.

expand to see more

The chronology is exact and worth stating plainly. Jesus constrained His disciples to get into the ship; He sent the multitudes away; He went up into a mountain to pray; and the ship was in the midst of the sea, tossed with waves, the wind contrary. They were in the storm because He put them there, and He was praying while they laboured. Against the common test — that a door which opens smoothly is God’s will and difficulty means a wrong turn — this narrative sets a storm entered by direct command. Paul was shipwrecked on the way to a destination God had promised him. The dictionary holds that circumstances are providence and providence is not self-interpreting; the will of God is known from His revealed word, and the road it puts a man on may be rough for reasons he learns later or never.

The two hospitality texts are the happier use and they are worth pressing on modern habits. The Emmaus disciples constrained a stranger to stay, and received the risen Christ at their table. Lydia argued the apostles into her house on the ground of her own new baptism — if ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord — which is a remarkable piece of reasoning from a woman converted that morning. Hebrews 13:2 says some have entertained angels unawares, and 1 Peter 4:9 commands hospitality without grudging. In an age where households are private and invitations are rare, this pressing, insistent, slightly inconvenient hospitality is a New Testament practice the church has quietly dropped.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parabiazomai (G3849), to constrain by entreaty, to urge strongly; anagkazo (G315), to compel, to necessitate; sunecho (G4912), to hold together, to press; Hebrew patsar (H6484), to urge, to press.

expand to see more

Greek parabiazomai (G3849) — to use force upon by entreaty; used only of the Emmaus disciples and of Lydia (Luke 24:29; Acts 16:15).

Greek anagkazo (G315) — to compel, to necessitate; Jesus constrained his disciples (Matthew 14:22) and Paul’s appeal to Caesar (Acts 28:19).

Greek sunecho (G4912) — to hold together, to press upon; the love of Christ constraineth us (2 Corinthians 5:14).

Hebrew patsar (H6484) — to press, to urge; used of Lot pressing the angels to turn in to his house (Genesis 19:3).

Greek ananke (G318) — necessity; necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:16).

Usage

"They constrained him, saying, Abide with us (Luke 24:29) — insistent hospitality, and the risen Christ at the table."

"And she constrained us (Acts 16:15) — a woman converted that morning arguing apostles into her house."

"Jesus constrained his disciples to get into a ship (Matthew 14:22) — sent by command into the storm that followed."
